extracted.intended_audience: readers of literary criticism; poets and creative writers seeking criteria for poetic greatness
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting the criteria by which a poet and a poem are judged great, as discussed in a literary-criticism essay comparing Dante and Shakespeare. Focuses on qualities of voice, form, moral depth, and lasting value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as "Musical Thought"
rubrics_metrics.description: "At the soul of all her voices and utterances was perfect music. Poetry, therefore, we will call musical Thought. The Poet is he who thinks in that manner."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry is fundamentally musical: the poet must think in terms of music and melody. If one can 'see deep enough' one finds music everywhere; the poetic utterance is essentially song-like and must exhibit inner musicality (Coleridge: musically worded sentences signal deep meaning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and Depth of Vision
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is a man's sincerity and depth of vision that makes him a Poet. See deep enough, and you see musically; the heart of Nature being everywhere music, if you can only reach it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True poetic value arises from authenticity and penetrating insight. Superficial cleverness or imitation ('the shows of great men') is inferior; the poet's inner truthfulness and profound perception determine poetic worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poem must be a Song; avoid unnecessary rhyme
rubrics_metrics.description: "All right Poems, Homer's and the rest, are authentically Songs. I would say, in strictness, that all right Poems are; that whatsoever is not sung is properly no Poem, but a piece of Prose cramped into jingling lines... I would advise all men who can speak their thought, not to sing it; to understand that, in a serious time, among serious men, there is no vocation in them for singing it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhyme and musical form are justified only when inwardly necessary to the thought; otherwise they become hollow jingling. The anti-pattern is rhyme without 'inward necessity'—a 'false song' or 'wooden noise.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensity (world-depth of vision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dante's prevailing character is 'intensity' — "His greatness has, in all senses, concentred itself into fiery emphasis and depth... He is world-great not because he is worldwide, but because he is world-deep."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great poets penetrate to the essential heart of things; greatness may be narrow in scope but extraordinarily deep in insight. Value is measured by concentrated inward force rather than mere breadth or encyclopaedic range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of Vision and Condensed Painting
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet 'seizes the very type of a thing; presents that and nothing more.' Examples: the Hall of Dite as a 'red-hot cone of iron,' Brunetto Latini's 'cotto aspetto,' 'fiery snow without wind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ability to discern and present the essential, emblematic image—brief, vivid, and decisive—is a mark of genius. Such painting is economy of sign and high pictorial precision; one 'smiting word' can suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity, Concision, and Silence as Eloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is a brevity, an abrupt precision in him... One smiting word; and then there is silence, nothing more said. His silence is more eloquent than words."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concise, decisive expression is prized: restraint and well-placed silence often communicate more than prolix explanation. Avoid surplusage; leave unessential matter aside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathy (empathic perception) and Sincerity in Representation
rubrics_metrics.description: "He must have been sincere about it too; sincere and sympathetic: a man without worth cannot give you the likeness of any object; he dwells in vague outwardness, fallacy and trivial hearsay... Find a man whose words paint you a likeness, you have found a man worth something."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To render a true likeness a poet must sympathize with the object and be sincere. Technical skill without inward sympathy yields only hearsay or trivial portraiture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Rigor Coupled with Genuine Pity
rubrics_metrics.description: "A man who does not know rigor cannot pity either. His very pity will be cowardly, egoistic,--sentimentality, or little better."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral strength and sternness are necessary to authentic compassion; sentimentality without rigor is shallow. Great poets balance stern judgment with profound pity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural Harmony and Structural Unity
rubrics_metrics.description: "A true inward symmetry, what one calls an architectural harmony, reigns in it, proportionates it all: architectural... The three kingdoms, Inferno, Purgatorio, Paradiso, look out on one another like compartments of a great edifice."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enduring works exhibit coherent structure and mutual support among parts; proportion and overall architectural balance (musical/architectural analogy) are essential. Parts should fit like hewn and polished stones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work Born of Painful, Earnest Labour
rubrics_metrics.description: "Thought, true labor of any kind, highest virtue itself, is it not the daughter of Pain?... This Book... has been written, in many senses, with his heart's blood."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great literature is often the product of intense, sustained effort and suffering; genuine creative labour (not casual or facile production) produces depth and durability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality and Timelessness via Inner Truth
rubrics_metrics.description: "For the thing that is uttered from the inmost parts of a man's soul, differs altogether from what is uttered by the outer part... True souls, in all generations of the world, who look on this Dante, will find a brotherhood in him; the deep sincerity of his thoughts... will speak likewise to their sincerity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that come from the inmost soul speak across ages and cultures; the test of endurance is inner veracity, not contemporary utility or popularity. Permanence springs from inward truth rather than outward circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of Form to Thought (speak plainly when possible)
rubrics_metrics.description: "I would advise all men who can speak their thought, not to sing it... Precisely as we love the true song, and are charmed by it as by something divine, so shall we hate the false song..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose form to suit necessity: if a thought can be spoken plainly, do not force it into verse or song. The poet should avoid ornamental form that obscures or substitutes for genuine thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to Embody a Civilization's Soul or Practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Dante 'embodies for us the Faith or soul' of medieval Europe; Shakespeare 'embodies for us the Outer Life... its chivalries, courtesies, humors, ambitions... the Practice or body.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A great poet may capture and render the defining inner life or outward practice of an era or people. Measure includes fidelity and comprehensiveness in embodying cultural reality—either spiritual (soul/faith) or practical (body/practice).
